Logic was forbidden because, as he put it, “logic is the gateway to philosophy, and the gateway to evil is itself evil.”
Philosophy, meanwhile, was evil itself. It was:

“the foundation of foolishness and dissolution, the source of confusion and error, and the cause of deviation and heresy (...) As for using the terminology of logic in questions of religious law, this is among the reprehensible and repulsive innovations and the newly introduced deviations. Religious law—praise be to God—has no need whatsoever for logic. As for what the logician claims about the usefulness of definition and demonstration, God has spared every sound mind any need for them...”
In his campaign against logic and philosophy, Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ even attacked Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī himself.
He objected to what al-Ghazālī wrote at the beginning of the introduction to al-Mustaṣfā. Speaking about logic, though without naming it directly, al-Ghazālī said:
“It is the introduction to all the sciences, and anyone who has not mastered it”—meaning this logical introduction—“cannot be trusted in any of his knowledge.”
Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ included this among his criticisms of al-Ghazālī in a statement on:
“important matters for which al-Ghazālī was criticized in his writings, and irregularities in his work that neither the scholars of his own school nor others approved.”
Al-Ghazālī’s remarks about logic were one of these “important matters.”
After Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, the banner of this traditionalist current was taken up by “Shaykh al-Islām” Taqī al-Dīn Aḥmad ibn al-ʿAbbās, better known as Ibn Taymiyya (661–729 AH).
For scholars of the intellectual heritage, Ibn Taymiyya’s name is closely associated with the two-front struggle he fought.
On one front, from his Hanbali position, he opposed the Ashʿarite school and the theological schools more generally.
On the other, he opposed Aristotelian logic and philosophy.

The basic principle behind Ibn Taymiyya’s method appears in the title The Agreement of Clear Reason with Authentic Revelation. The idea is that everything reliably transmitted in the Islamic texts must necessarily agree with reason.
For Ibn Taymiyya, then, there can be no real conflict between reason and revealed law.
If a conflict appears, the transmitted text must be unreliable. But if a genuine conflict remains even though the text is authentic, then the text—not reason—must be the final authority.
He built his arguments on both fronts around this principle.
Ibn Taymiyya did not, however, take an absolutely negative position toward logic. Unlike Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, he did not simply forbid people from studying it.
Instead, in a number of his works, he examined the foundations of Aristotelian logic and the ways it had been applied in the arguments of Muslim theologians from different schools.
Here too, his criticism returns to the same basic principle.
For Ibn Taymiyya, the logic of the Aristotelians conflicted with authentic Islamic texts. In his system, this necessarily meant that it also conflicted with sound reason.
His overall criticism of Aristotelian logic and of the Muslim theologians who used it centers on two main questions: definition and syllogism.
This form of logic was concerned with organizing the ways in which two kinds of knowledge could be reached: knowledge of concepts and knowledge of judgments.
It made definition the route to knowledge of concepts, and syllogism the route to knowledge of judgments.
Ibn Taymiyya rejects both claims. He denies that Aristotelian definition is the necessary route to the first kind of knowledge, and that Aristotelian syllogism is the necessary route to the second.
He therefore also rejects the Aristotelians’ claim that concepts can be reached only through definition and judgments only through syllogism.

“All these claims are false, both in what they deny and in what they affirm. Not everything they reject in the methods of others is false, and not everything they affirm in their own methods is true in the way they claim.”

The most important arguments Ibn Taymiyya uses against Aristotelian definition are connected with his view of the relation between essence and existence—or, more plainly, between the universal and the particular.
He draws a sharp line between essence—the universal or general—and existence outside the mind.
For him, essence exists only in the mind. Outside the mind, only particulars exist: the individual, concrete instances of an essence.

Abstract essences therefore have no independent existence outside the mind, as they do in Plato’s theory of Forms. Nor do they exist alongside individual things in the way they do for Aristotle and the Muslim Aristotelians.
Ibn Taymiyya thus breaks the real connection between the universal and the particular. The first exists only in the mind; the second exists only in the external world.
This is the basis of his objection to the Aristotelian idea of logical definition.
For the Aristotelians, a true definition is made up of the essential qualities of the thing being defined. Those essential qualities form part of the thing’s essence.
In Ibn Taymiyya’s view, however, this would mean that the essences of things—their true realities—must themselves exist outside the mind.

It would also mean, first, that this external existence was different from their existence in the mind, and second, that it was different from the concrete existence of the individual things in which those essences appeared.
Ibn Taymiyya describes these supposed consequences as separating an essence from its existence—by which he means its existence in the mind.
All this means that the source of his objection is his opposition to what he sees as the consequences of believing in fixed, abstract essences.
One possible consequence is the existence of eternal essences in a world above nature, as in Plato’s Forms. This would mean accepting a plurality of eternal realities.

The other is the idea of an eternal essence of matter—prime matter—that exists potentially before becoming actual through form. This, in turn, leads to the claim that the material world is eternal, as implied by Aristotle’s theory of matter and form in his “first philosophy.”
Both conclusions conflict with Islamic doctrine: the first with the unity of God, and the second with the belief that the world was created in time.
Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of Aristotelian logical definition is therefore religious in its basis. It follows from his principle that clear reason must agree with authentic revelation.
It is not a purely logical criticism. In other words, it does not begin by examining the idea of definition simply as a problem within logic.

We should nevertheless recognize that Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of the distinction made by Peripatetic logicians between essential and accidental qualities in definitions has a positive side and comes closer to reality.
It leads him to reject fixed essences understood in an idealist and metaphysical sense.

But his criticism still rests mainly on his decision to break the real connection between an essence and its concrete instances in the external world, because he confines the existence of essence to the mind.
The second main target of Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of Aristotelian logic is the syllogism.
Here he goes into considerable detail. Some of his arguments concern the propositions used to build a demonstration, while others concern the methods of logical inference themselves.
When discussing propositions, Ibn Taymiyya makes a major effort to establish the certainty of particular propositions based on experience and of reports transmitted through many independent chains.
His aim is to establish the certainty of ḥadīth in the Islamic sense and thereby support his basic principle: the agreement of clear reason with authentic revelation.

He criticizes philosophers for refusing to recognize widely transmitted reports as a source of certain knowledge. In his view, they restrict certain knowledge to theoretical propositions—that is, propositions produced through rational logical syllogism.
He also rejects the philosophers’ claim that certain knowledge is produced by rational logical demonstration and that the propositions produced by such demonstration must be universal.
Here again, his criticism follows from his belief that universals exist only in the mind and that only individual, concrete things exist outside it.
If that is true, then logical demonstration cannot give us knowledge of anything that actually exists in the external world.

“What perfection does the soul gain simply by conceiving these general and universal things if it does not conceive the particular, concrete beings that actually exist? And what knowledge of the Lord of the worlds can there be in this, when the soul can reach perfection only by knowing Him and worshipping Him with love and submission?”
The source of Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism here is the belief that God is a specific, individual reality rather than a universal.
A universal implies a plurality of individual instances, and this would conflict with the doctrine of divine unity.
Ibn Taymiyya therefore concludes that universal knowledge cannot be certain and that logical demonstration does not provide real knowledge.
The error in all these equations, however, lies in the foundation on which Ibn Taymiyya builds them.
He denies that essences, or universals, exist in the external world within particular things.

In other words, the basic weakness in all these arguments is that he has no scientific solution to the problem of how the universal and the particular—the general and the specific—are related in reality.
This is why Ibn Taymiyya continues trying to prove that the universal premises used in Aristotelian logical demonstration are neither truly universal nor truly certain.
Yet after all the effort he puts into rejecting reliance on universal propositions, he is not troubled by contradicting himself in two other statements.
The first concerns religious questions. Here he says:

“In matters known through the sayings of the prophets, the need for a universal proposition becomes clear. One example of such a universal proposition is the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him, that every intoxicant is forbidden.”

“Grasping the universal is one of the most distinctive qualities of reason, by which it differs from the senses. The senses know only a particular thing, while reason understands it universally and without restriction.”
But even this recognition of universal propositions is connected with a strongly sensory and empirical position.

In his reply to the logicians, Ibn Taymiyya argues that particular items of knowledge—knowledge gained through the senses—are the only realities that actually exist in the particular things of the external world.
From this he concludes that universals are of no real use because they exist only in the mind.

His final conclusion is that the knowledge produced by logical demonstration is not knowledge of what actually exists. It is knowledge only of something purely mental, with no reality outside the mind.

As for Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of the methods of Aristotelian logical inference, it is built in general on the same foundations as his criticism of Aristotelian definition in the formation of concepts and his criticism of the propositions that make up—and are produced by—demonstration in the Aristotelian theory of judgments.
In fact, many Muslim theologians and scholars of legal theory took a similar position toward Aristotelian logic because of their position on the problem of definition.

They feared the consequences that might follow for Islamic metaphysics if they accepted a theory of definition based on fixed essences. We saw this clearly in our discussion of Ibn Taymiyya’s position.
After Ibn Taymiyya, two currents appeared among the traditionalists.
One continued in his general direction.
The other followed the Ashʿarite line, opposing philosophy and philosophers with the weapons of philosophy itself.

Within the first current, some returned to Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ’s method of simply forbidding logic and philosophy. Among them were Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya (d. 751 AH), al-Ṣanʿānī (d. 840 AH), and al-Suyūṭī (d. 911 AH).
The second current—the Ashʿarite one—eventually included later thinkers who practiced philosophical reasoning quite freely.
Some modern researchers have described their method by saying that they:

“became deeply immersed in philosophical books, until the subject matter of the two sciences—kalām and philosophy—became confused for them and they treated the two as one. Questions of kalām became mixed with questions of philosophy until the two disciplines could no longer be clearly distinguished, as happened with al-Bayḍāwī (d. 691 AH/1286 CE) in al-Ṭawāliʿ and ʿAḍud al-Dīn al-Ījī (d. 750 AH/1355 CE) in al-Mawāqif.”

The general pattern in how earlier writers approached the philosophical heritage after Ibn Taymiyya, well beyond the sixteenth century, was shaped by these two currents, despite some very important exceptions.
The Ashʿarite current, however, generally kept its dominant position in intellectual activity in this field.
Most of the major later commentators on theological and philosophical works, and most historians of philosophy, were Ashʿarites, from Ibn Khaldūn to Ṭāshkubrīzāda (d. 963 AH/1550 CE).
Among the important exceptions were the later Shiʿi philosophers, above all Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, better known as Mullā Ṣadrā or Ṣadr al-Mutaʾallihīn (980–1050 AH/1573–1640 CE).
They are exceptions in two senses.
First, these Shiʿi philosophers approached philosophical thought from outside both of the currents discussed above—the Hanbali and the Ashʿarite—at least in terms of their formal school affiliation.
Second, their approach to philosophy had a strong internal consistency.
This was possible because they developed its metaphysical categories and concepts in ways that matched Shiʿi concepts, especially those concerning prophecy and the Imamate.
For this reason, Shiʿi philosophical activity in the later period of the classical tradition was not only intellectually fertile. It also developed features of its own.
